doc.title: Dick Katz interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 7, 2002

title: Fats Waller, Basie records and first gigs
summary: Waller as his first inspiration, playing for him at the Royal, discovering Basie and Lester Young, a high school band and Baltimore gigs; a digression on Minton's and Carmen McRae.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: play, I would watch her hands and imitate her. So it didn’t really take, but let’s see, the first one to turn me on was Fats Waller. My brother had these Fats Waller records. And the way he played the piano, still, if you listen, it had an equilibrium and a balance, it’s very rare even now. And there were certain little figures. I didn’t really — I tried a little bit to play like him, but like a lot of kids I would just imitate little licks here and there. And early on I realized well I’m not really ever going to be a real stride player. And I had one experience which I wrote about and I wrote the notes to — oh I’m skipping around now a little bit — but one of the first in quotes big time experiences I had was working at Minton’s Playhouse, the fabled Minton’s Playhouse with a clarinetist named Tony Scott. And I really liked — trial by fire with Philly Joe Jones and Milt Hinton and Tony, and the girl singer was Carmen McRae. So I made one of her first records, it was called something — I forgot the name. Anyhow the two albums I did with her have been reissued from Decca and I wrote — I was asked to write the notes for them. So in writing the notes I told this story about the Royal Theater and Fats Waller and all this stuff. Now wait a minute now, let me get this straight. I don’t know if it was for that LP or not, I’m trying to remember which. I really should cancel this segment. I’ll tell you why, because I want to get it right. What I’m getting at is the story about Fats Waller, was I was asked — this older record collector friend of mine who still lives down there, used to go down to the Royal and when all those big names would come in he would hang around backstage and present them with rare 78s they’d forgotten they’d even made. So he dragged me along one day and he made me play for Fats. I was about 16 or 17, in the basement of the theater. So I wrote about that. And he was one of the first. And then one day when I was about 13 or 14 he had left this stack of records on top of the record player, my brother, and he says, “Don’t you dare ever touch those if I’m not here.” Of course I did. So the first ones I pulled off were the first Count Basie records on Decca. Okay? I put it on. When I heard that rhythm section and Lester Young, the whole thing turned around. Just grabbed me. Whatever that was, I wanted to go that way. So experiences like that helped me and I used to go down, as I got a little older and I was learning to play, teach myself to play a little bit, I had a friend a trombone player and we would play and I used to play in a high school band, we used to play stock arrangements. You’ll hear this experience a lot too from other musicians from local bands. And I worked little gigs around Baltimore. I knew about four tunes.
But were you reading like chord symbols at the time? Could you do that?
Mostly finding your part by ear?
